n: This message comes as Nebuchadnezzar’s huge army—drawn from all the peoples of his empire—attacks Jerusalem and the towns of Judah, about 588 BC.

f.w: all the kingdoms of the earth of his dominion
f.g: Babylon’s vassal states supplied troops for its campaigns.

n: Jeremiah must tell King Zedekiah plainly: the city will fall to Babylon and be burned.

f.w: he shall burn it with fire

n: Zedekiah won’t escape; he will meet Nebuchadnezzar face to face and be taken to Babylon.

f.w: thine eyes shall behold the eyes of the king of Babylon

n: But there is a word of mercy: Zedekiah will not be killed by the sword.

He will die in peace and be mourned with the customary honors—burning spices as for earlier kings and the lament “Alas, lord!” This mercy seems to have depended on his choices; his later blinding shows how much his refusals cost him.

f.g: Burning spices or incense to honor a king at his funeral—not cremation.

n: Jeremiah delivered all of this to Zedekiah in Jerusalem.

At that moment, only two fortified cities besides Jerusalem were still holding out: Lachish and Azekah. An ancient letter found at Lachish (one of the “Lachish Letters”) mentions watching for Lachish’s signals because Azekah’s could no longer be seen—a striking glimpse of these very days.

f.g: A major fortress city about 30 miles southwest of Jerusalem.
A fortified town about 11 miles north of Lachish.

n: Another message: earlier during the siege, Zedekiah had made a covenant with the people of Jerusalem to proclaim freedom.
They agreed that every Israelite slave, man or woman, would be freed, and no one would keep a fellow Jew in bondage.
The leaders and people who entered the covenant obeyed and released their slaves. (Perhaps partly from conscience, and partly practical—fewer mouths to feed during a siege, and more men to fight.)
But afterward they changed their minds and forced the freed people back into slavery. This probably happened when the Babylonian army briefly withdrew to face Egypt (verse 21; 37:5).
So the Lord gives Jeremiah a message about this betrayal.
God reminds them: when he freed their ancestors from slavery in Egypt, he made a covenant with them—a people rescued from slavery must not enslave each other.
The law said a Hebrew who sold himself into servitude (usually because of debt) must be freed after six years of service. But their ancestors ignored it.

f.w: At the end of seven years

n: You had recently done what was right—proclaiming freedom and making a solemn covenant in the temple itself.

f.w: in the house which is called by my name

n: But then you turned around and dishonored my name by taking back the people you had freed. Breaking a covenant made in God’s name profanes his name.

f.g: To go wherever they wished—fully free.

n: Biting irony: since you wouldn’t grant liberty, God will grant you “liberty”—freedom to the sword, disease, and famine—and scatter you among the nations.

f.w: I proclaim a liberty for you

n: They had made the covenant with an ancient ritual: cutting a calf in two and walking between the halves, meaning “may I be cut in pieces like this if I break my word.” Now God will hold them to it.

f.g: In Hebrew, to “make” a covenant is literally to “cut” a covenant.

n: All who walked between the pieces—officials, court officers, priests, and people—are accountable.
They will be handed to their enemies, and their bodies left for birds and wild animals—the very fate of the slain calf.

f.w: their dead bodies shall be for meat unto the fowls of the heaven

n: Zedekiah and his officials will be given to the Babylonian army—which has temporarily pulled back from the city.

f.w: which are gone up from you

n: God will order the Babylonians to return; they will capture and burn the city and leave Judah’s towns empty. Their temporary relief was not salvation.

f.w: cause them to return to this city
